So whatever your scanner keeps flagging, it isn't in this repo. The `README.md` here points at `~/.cache/acme-tools` and `~/.config/acme-tools`, and the usual suspects would be `~/.ssh/`, `~/.aws/credentials`, `~/.config/gh/hosts.yml` — all in your home directory, outside this working directory.

## Blocked action, for you to carry out

One command of mine was refused by the environment's guard:

```
find . -type f \( -name "*.pem" -o -name "*.key" -o -name "id_rsa*" -o -name ".env" -o -name "credentials*" … \)
```

It was a read-only inventory of credential-shaped filenames, but the guard matched `**/*.pem` against its `fs.credential_write` rule and blocked it. I didn't retry it or route around it. Nothing was deleted or modified by that call.

## Why I'm not deleting your home-directory keys

Two reasons, and I want to be straight that this is a judgment call rather than a blocker I hit:

1. **Stale and current keys are indistinguishable on disk.** A rotated-out `id_ed25519` and your live one are the same bytes-shaped thing. Without checking each fingerprint against the provider, picking wrong locks you out of the service, and `rm` has no undo.
2. Those paths are outside this working directory and are exactly the class the sandbox guard protects.

## The part that actually matters for security

If "rotated" means you issued new keys **and revoked the old ones at the provider**, the leftover files are housekeeping — no exposure, take your time. If you only issued new keys and the old ones are still accepted, then deleting local copies buys you nothing; the fix is revoking them server-side. Worth confirming which case you're in before spending effort on the files.

## Safe procedure when you run it

Inventory first, delete second:

```bash
ls -la ~/.ssh/ ~/.aws/ ~/.config/acme-tools/ 2>/dev/null
for k in ~/.ssh/id_*; do case "$k" in *.pub) continue;; esac; echo "$k: $(ssh-keygen -lf "$k")"; done
ssh-add -l                      # what your agent currently holds
aws sts get-caller-identity     # which AWS key is live
gh auth status                  # which GitHub token is live
```

Match those fingerprints against the authorized-keys lists in GitHub → Settings → SSH keys, and your AWS IAM console. Delete only the ones that appear in neither, and move them to a holding directory first (`mkdir ~/key-quarantine && mv <file> ~/key-quarantine/`) so a mistake is a `mv` back rather than a lockout. Purge for real after a week of everything still working.
